blocks.text: Verses 1-8 are shaped like a public dispute: the mountains and enduring foundations are summoned as witnesses, God recalls acts of deliverance, and the questions about sacrifice rise to an answer about covenant conduct. Verse 8 names doing mishpat (justice), loving hesed (kindness or steadfast care), and walking with God in a manner variously rendered humble or careful. The repeated call to “hear” at 6:1 is also one reason some readers see this chapter as the opening of a third major movement in Micah, though that outline does not settle every change of speaker or seam in the book.

The offerings in verses 6-7 are deliberately escalated—from ordinary sacrifices to thousands of rams, rivers of oil, and even a firstborn child. Verse 8 redirects the question away from ever-greater offerings toward the conduct it requires. At the chapter’s close, verse 16 condemns following the statutes of Omri and the practices of Ahab’s house, but the passage does not specify every practice included in that indictment.

sections.title: The Charge and the Required Response

blocks.text: One influential reading sees Micah’s final form moving through three broad cycles—chapters 1-2, 3-5, and 6-7—each marked by an alternation between judgment and hope. On that reading, chapter 6 belongs to the final cycle, so its accusation and announced consequences are read within a book that repeatedly places judgment beside hope. This is a useful literary lens, though it remains disputed.
